title: My Health Records Amendment (Strengthening Privacy) Bill 2018
short_title: My Health Records Amendment (Strengthening Privacy) Bill 2018

divisions.question: The majority voted against a motion introduced by Labor MP [Catherine King](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/ballarat/catherine_king), which would have amended the usual [second reading motion](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html) "that the bill be read a second time" (which is parliamentary jargon for agreeing with the main idea of the bill) and replace it with the following: > *That all words after "That" be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:* > *"whilst not declining to give the bill a second reading, the House calls on the Government to suspend the 'opt out' phase of the My Health Record rollout until other privacy and security concerns are addressed."*

The majority voted against [amendments](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2018-11-14.19.1) made by Senator [Helen Polley](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/tasmania/helen_polley) (Tas), which means they failed. Senator Polley [explained that](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2018-11-14.19.2): > *Labor's view is that 12 months is needed to amend the legislation and to undertake and implement a Privacy Commissioner review of concerns that can't be fixed by legislation. The very open default access setting and the automatic uploading of two years of Medicare PBS data communicate these additional protections to all Australians to rebuild the trust and confidence in My Health Record. Of course, any extension is an improvement on what the government was offering this morning, but it is imperative that we get this right.* ### Motion text > *(1) Clause 3, page 2 (after line 11), at the end of the clause, add:* >> *Note: The provisions of the My Health Records (National Application) Rules2017 amended or inserted by this Act, and any other provisions of those rules, may be amended or repealed by rules made under section 109 of the My Health Records Act 2012 (see subsection 13(5) of the Legislation Act 2003).* > *(2) Schedule 1, page 9 (after line 12), at the end of the Schedule, add:* >> *My Health Records (National Application) Rules 2017* >> *18 Paragraph 6 ( 3 ) (b)* >> *Omit "4 months", substitute "16 months".*

speeches.speaker: Greg Hunt
speeches.brief: The My Health Records Amendment (Strengthening Privacy) Bill 2018 was introduced to enhance privacy protections for the My Health Record system, which has over six million Australians and 13,000 healthcare provider organisations participating, with nearly seven million clinical documents and 22 million prescription documents uploaded.

speeches.speaker: David Gillespie
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the My Health Records Amendment (Strengthening Privacy) Bill 2018, arguing it strengthens privacy protections and allows permanent deletion of records, noting that six million people enrolled under the previous opt-in system with no law enforcement access.

speeches.speaker: Chris Hayes
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the My Health Records Amendment (Strengthening Privacy) Bill 2018 and moved two amendments to prevent misuse in pre-employment and family violence contexts, calling for the opt-out period to be suspended until security concerns are addressed, while criticising the government's botched rollout and noting six million people had already opted into the scheme.

speeches.speaker: Susan Lamb
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the government should suspend the My Health Record rollout until remaining privacy and safety concerns are fixed, including risks to domestic violence victims and potential employer discrimination, and noted the bill addresses some issues but not all.

speeches.speaker: Joanne Ryan
speeches.brief: Labor will support the My Health Record privacy bill and move amendments in the Senate, but argues the government’s switch from an opt‑in to an opt‑out system has created a trust deficit that can only be fixed by reverting to an opt‑in model.

speeches.speaker: Stephen Jones
speeches.brief: The MP supported the My Health Records Amendment (Strengthening Privacy) Bill 2018, arguing the My Health Record scheme saves lives and money, while welcoming amendments requiring court orders for law-enforcement or government access and permanent deletion of records for those who opt out. He also criticised the government for mishandling the rollout and urged against abandoning the scheme amid privacy concerns.

speeches.speaker: Ed Husic
speeches.brief: The government's opt-out model for My Health Record failed to build public trust, and its history of digital project failures—including the 2016 census crash and robo-debt—undermines confidence. The bill needs stronger privacy protections, informed consent, and an extended opt-out period to prevent data misuse by insurers, employers, and third parties.

speeches.speaker: Matt Thistlethwaite
speeches.brief: The speaker supported amendments to the My Health Records Amendment (Strengthening Privacy) Bill 2018, arguing the government bungled the $1.2 billion rollout and that the bill should go further—requiring court orders for law enforcement access, permanent deletion of records after opt-out, and extending protections to insurance companies, employer discrimination, and family violence.

speeches.speaker: Anne Stanley
speeches.brief: The Labor MP argued that the government has mishandled the My Health Record rollout, criticising the shift to an opt-out system and insufficient privacy protections, and called for suspending the opt-out period and a Senate inquiry. They welcomed the bill's requirement for court orders to access records and permanent deletion for opt-outs, but said it fails to protect vulnerable Australians, and also cited $2.8 billion in hospital cuts since 2014.

speeches.speaker: Tony Zappia
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the government’s mismanagement of the My Health Record system has caused over 900,000 Australians to opt out, with likely more than one million by 15 November, and that the bill does not address key privacy concerns such as access to records of children aged 14–18, family separation cases, employer access, and pharmaceutical company use.

speeches.speaker: Emma McBride
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the My Health Records Amendment bill is welcome but insufficient, calling for the opt-out period to be suspended until privacy concerns are resolved, noting 900,000 Australians have already opted out and that digital health records could save $11.5 billion over 15 years.

speeches.speaker: Sharon Claydon
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the My Health Record Amendment (Strengthening Privacy) Bill 2018 and amendments by the member for Ballarat, but argued the bill does not go far enough. They announced Labor would establish a separate inquiry into broader issues, including the opt-out system, privacy protections for domestic violence victims and employees, and third-party data access, with a report due 8 October.

speeches.speaker: Justine Elliot
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the government has botched the My Health Record rollout, calling it a debacle that reflects broader dysfunction, and cited failures with the NBN and NDIS as further examples of poor IT and program management.

speeches.speaker: Rebekha Sharkie
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the My Health Records Amendment (Strengthening Privacy) Bill 2018, citing benefits such as nationwide access to medical records, instant access for healthcare professionals, and a centralised database linking Medicare, PBS and the donor registry. They noted over 900,000 people had opted out since July, raised concerns about data security risks including breaches in Singapore, the US and the UK, and argued the opt-out system could leave many unaware their records were created, while also highlighting risks to victims of family violence due to inadequate safeguards and conflicting definitions of parental responsibility.

speeches.speaker: Luke Howarth
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the My Health Records Amendment (Strengthening Privacy) Bill 2018 gives consumers control over their health information, listing three benefits: emergency access, a convenient health snapshot, and personal record control. He noted nearly six million people have opted in, with only three percent opting out, and encouraged constituents to sign up via my.gov.au.

speeches.speaker: John Alexander
speeches.brief: The My Health Records Amendment (Strengthening Privacy) Bill 2018 removes the ability to disclose health information to law enforcement or government bodies without a court order or consent, requires deletion of records for consumers who cancel, and extends the opt-out period to 15 November 2018.

speeches.speaker: Russell Broadbent
speeches.brief: The speaker argued in favour of the My Health Records Amendment (Strengthening Privacy) Bill 2018, urging unanimous support to improve health outcomes through shared patient information. He cited personal anecdotes of adverse drug reactions and the benefits for travellers, noting that six million Australians are already enrolled, and framed the bill as a common-sense measure to reduce hospital admissions and healthcare duplication.

speeches.speaker: Bert Van Manen
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the My Health Records Amendment (Strengthening Privacy) Bill 2018, arguing it would improve efficiency, reduce costs, and enhance medical care by strengthening privacy protections, and noted that six million Australians have already signed up for the system.

acts.title: My Health Records Amendment (Strengthening Privacy) Act 2018
